source_acquisition.search_note: PDF p.3 explicitly links the repository. gh read-only metadata description and README title exactly match the paper; README maps heuristic, energy, CPT and Appendix C.2 notebooks to the figures. The local compact source directory was checked first; GH main tree was then read without cloning or modifying the repository. No paper TeX layout source is present, so final panel merges/captions are taken from the verified PDF.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Categorical HUSL for top-p in heuristic plots; Set2 for model identity in random-split Figure 1; crest sequential hues for old margin rho_o in CDFs; blue/green categorical pair for generation/verification energy.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Rendered PDF is vector-dominant: pdfimages reports no embedded raster images; figures combine vector paths, PDF font objects and semi-transparent vector bands/points.
paper_style.style_consistency: Computer Modern/TeX, thin despined axes, no background grid, shared legends and repeated HUSL/crest grammars are consistent. Main weaknesses are symlog axes, hidden facet ticks and dependence on shared color legends.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Misreporting the tokenization of outputs generated by different LLMs using Algorithm 1. Panel (a) shows the percentage of tokens overcharged by an unfaithful provider who misreports the tokenization of the outputs to 600 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform using Algorithm 1, for different values of m. Panel (b) shows the fraction of outputs to the same 600 prompts where Algorithm 1 returns a tokenization that is plausible under top-p sampling, for different values of m. In both panels, we set the temperature to 1.3 and use top-p sampling with p = 0.95. In panel (b), we repeat the experiment 5 times to obtain 90% confidence intervals.

encodings.x: Number of iterations m (0-1300 in a; 0-100 in b)
encodings.shape: circle markers in panel b only

figures.data_and_statistics: 600 LMSYS Chatbot Arena prompts; T=1.3, top-p p=0.95. Panel (a) aggregates extra reported tokens under random splitting; panel (b) aggregates fraction of outputs still plausible and shows 5-repeat 90% intervals.
figures.evidence_relation: §3.1 Algorithm 1 establishes the no-GPU length incentive; §3.2 uses plausibility as the suspicion constraint. The paired panels motivate the later hardness theorem and Algorithm 2.
design_strengths: Places reward and plausibility on a shared m axis.
Caption defines sample, sampling settings, and interval construction.
design_weaknesses: Only panel (b) carries an uncertainty band.
External/shared model legend is required after panel cropping; color is not redundant in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair an incentive curve with a detectability/plausibility curve over the same operational knob.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Additional revenue from misreporting the tokenization of outputs using Algorithm 2. The panels show the percentage of tokens overcharged by an unfaithful provider who misreports the tokenization of the outputs generated by an LLM to 600 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform using the reporting policies pi_m^H implemented by Algorithm 2 for different values of m and p. The dashed vertical lines correspond to the optimal value of m. Here, we set the temperature of the model to 1.3 and repeat each experiment 5 times to obtain 90% confidence intervals. Refer to Appendix C.1 for additional results using alternative temperature values and other LLMs.

color.semantic_mapping: HUSL: p=0.99 blue, p=0.95 green, p=0.90 pink

encodings.text: model names below panels; shared p legend

figures.data_and_statistics: 600 LMSYS prompts, T=1.3; three p values and m sweeps. y is percentage of extra reported tokens; 5 repeats yield 90% confidence bands. Dashed guides identify the maximizing m for each p.
figures.evidence_relation: Algorithm 2 output is evaluated after §3.2 hardness; Figure 2 is the empirical overcharge input to Eq. (4) and Figure 3, with Appendix C.1 expanding model/temperature coverage.
design_strengths: Shared color grammar and explicit optimum guides make the policy choice visible.
Symlog retains both near-zero and roughly 10% effects.
design_weaknesses: Symlog zero neighborhood is harder to read than a linear axis.
Only the left y-axis is labeled; the metric name ‘additional revenue’ requires caption interpretation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Facet by model, color the plausibility threshold, and mark the chosen operating point with same-color reference lines.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Financial gain from misreporting the tokenization of outputs using Algorithm 2. The panels show the utility gain that an unfaithful provider who misreports the tokenization of the outputs generated by an LLM to 600 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform using Algorithm 2 can achieve, for different values of p and the provider's profit margin rho_o. The dashed vertical lines represent the minimum margin above which misreporting is financially viable according to Eq. 4. Here, for each value of p, we run Algorithm 2 using the optimal number of iterations m shown in Figure 2, set the temperature of the model to 1.3 and repeat each experiment 5 times to obtain 90% confidence intervals. Refer to Figure 7 of Appendix C.1 for additional results using alternative temperature values and other LLMs.

encodings.y: Increase in utility (%) on symlog/log-like scale
encodings.line: solid utility curve; dashed viability threshold
encodings.text: model names below panels; p legend

figures.data_and_statistics: 600 LMSYS prompts; T=1.3; m selected from Figure 2 per p; y is relative utility gain over truthful pi_0. Five repeats provide 90% bands; vertical guides are Eq. (4) minimum viable margins.
figures.evidence_relation: Combines Figure 2's optimum with Appendix C.3 energy ratio c_o/c_v through Eq. (4), testing whether overcharge outweighs verification cost. It is the central heuristic-to-utility link before the pricing prescription.
design_strengths: Places theoretical viability threshold and empirical utility in one coordinate system.
Keeps Figure 2's model/color ordering for direct comparison.
design_weaknesses: Symlog and zero-truncated positive segments obscure small gains.
Band reflects repeated runs, not a full prompt-level distribution; only three models are shown.
figures.reusable_pattern: Choose m in the revenue plot, then propagate that choice into a utility curve with a same-color cost threshold.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Provider's profit margin under a pay-per-character pricing mechanism. The panels show, across different models and different values rho_o of the provider's profit margin under pay-per-token, the (empirical) cumulative distribution function of their profit margin rho(t) = 1 - c_gen(t)/r(t) per output t after their transition to pay-per-character. Here, we first compute the average ratio of number of tokens to number of characters (tpc) across the responses of each model to 600 multilingual prompts sampled from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena dataset, with sampling proportional to each language's frequency. Then, we set r_c = r_o * tpc and compute the provider's profit margin rho(t) for outputs to 600 different multilingual prompts. In all panels, dashed vertical lines show empirical averages of the respective distributions, and we set the temperature of the models to 1.3 and use top-p sampling with p = 0.95.

color.semantic_mapping: crest: rho_o=0.2 pale green, 0.4 teal, 0.6 navy

encodings.line: solid step CDF; dashed empirical mean
encodings.text: model names below panels; shared rho_o legend

figures.data_and_statistics: 600 multilingual prompts to estimate tpc per model and a different 600 multilingual prompts to compute per-output margin after r_c=r_o*tpc; T=1.3, top-p=.95. CDFs expose negative-margin tails.
figures.evidence_relation: Theorem 6/Corollary 7 prescribe character-linear pricing; Figure 4 tests the realized per-output margin distribution and feeds the discussion of heterogeneous margins.
design_strengths: CDF keeps tail risk visible rather than collapsing to an average.
Same-color mean guides connect target old margin with realized distribution.
design_weaknesses: No interval or sampling uncertainty is encoded for the empirical CDF.
Shared legend and hidden per-panel labels reduce standalone portability.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use an empirical CDF plus same-color target/mean reference to show both average preservation and per-output risk.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Fraction of outputs for which Algorithm 2 finds a longer plausible tokenization. The figure shows the fraction of outputs generated by different LLMs to 600 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform for which Algorithm 2 finds a longer plausible tokenization under top-p sampling, for values of m, p and temperature. We repeat each experiment 5 times to calculate 90% confidence intervals.

color.semantic_mapping: HUSL: p=.99/.95/.90; model and temperature are facets

encodings.text: row model labels, bottom temperature labels, shared p legend

figures.data_and_statistics: 9 facets for Llama-1B, Gemma-1B, Ministral-8B across T=1.45/1.30/1.15; each uses 600 prompts, three p values, and 5-repeat 90% intervals.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix C.1 extends Figure 2's plausibility premise beyond T=1.3 and the three main-text model panels, supporting the claim that higher p/temperature increase plausible longer tokenizations.
design_strengths: Fixed facet geometry makes temperature/model sensitivity comparable.
Retains the main HUSL and band grammar.
design_weaknesses: Nine small panels hide most tick labels and crowd overlapping curves.
Caption says different LLMs but leaves the concrete row list to the grid labels.
figures.reusable_pattern: Make two experimental knobs facets and reserve a stable color legend for the third knob.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Additional revenue from misreporting the tokenization of outputs using Algorithm 2. The panels show the percentage of tokens overcharged by an unfaithful provider who misreports the tokenization of the outputs generated by several LLMs to 600 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform using Algorithm 2, for different values of m, p and temperature. The dashed lines highlight the optimal value of m. We repeat each experiment 5 times to obtain 90% confidence intervals.

encodings.text: row model labels, bottom temperature labels

figures.data_and_statistics: 15 model×temperature facets, 600 prompts per condition, p=.99/.95/.90 and m sweeps; each curve uses 5 repeats and 90% interval bands. Dashed guides mark optimal m.
figures.evidence_relation: This is the full-model/temperature extension of Figure 2; the optimal-m grammar remains the operational bridge from Algorithm 2 to utility in Figure 7.
design_strengths: Full five-model coverage while preserving Figure 2 grammar.
Per-condition peak guides expose how optimum moves with p and temperature.
design_weaknesses: High-density symlog grid is costly to inspect.
Many panels suppress labels; color is the sole p encoding.
figures.reusable_pattern: Repeat the headline plot's policy-selection grammar across a controlled model×temperature grid.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Financial gain from misreporting the tokenization of outputs using Algorithm 2. The panels show the financial gain that an unfaithful provider who misreports the tokenization of the outputs generated by several LLMs to 600 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform using Algorithm 2 can achieve, as a function of the profit margin on the output tokens rho_o and p. The dashed vertical lines represent the minimum margin under which misreporting is financially viable according to Eq. 4. Here, for each value of p, we select the optimal number of iterations m in Algorithm 2 shown on Figure 2, and repeat each experiment 5 times to obtain 90% confidence intervals.

encodings.y: Increase in utility (%) on symlog/log-like scale
encodings.line: solid utility curve; dashed Eq.-4 threshold
encodings.text: row/column labels plus shared p legend

figures.data_and_statistics: 15 model×temperature facets; m is selected from Figure 2 for each p, then utility gain is evaluated over rho_o using energy ratio and 5-repeat 90% bands. Dashed lines are Eq. (4) viability thresholds.
figures.evidence_relation: Completes the expanded Figure 6 → utility link, combining heuristic plausibility, optimal m and C.3 energy costs. It is the appendix counterpart of Figure 3.
design_strengths: Threshold lines make financial viability explicit in every condition.
Stable facets permit direct Figure 6-to-7 comparison.
design_weaknesses: Symlog, threshold lines and near-zero curves overlap in low-gain cells.
Caption does not restate each model's energy ratio or sample split.
figures.reusable_pattern: Select the policy in one facet grid and carry it into a second grid whose reference line encodes the decision boundary.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Responses to the prompt “is Dead Snow worth watching or should I watch directly Dead Snow 2?”.

color.semantic_mapping: black token text/borders; red split points and iteration numbers; gray outlines

encodings.color: red split markers vs black tokens
encodings.line: vertical token separators; red split separators

figures.data_and_statistics: One Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct output example at p=.95, T=1.3; the lower sequence preserves the decoded string while splitting three token locations until the first non-plausible state.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix C.2 makes Algorithm 2's string-preserving transformation concrete; it is a qualitative companion to aggregate plausibility/overcharge curves in Figures 1–2.
design_strengths: Paired boxes make the invariant string and changed token boundaries easy to compare.
Iteration numbers expose operation order.
design_weaknesses: Caption gives only the prompt; setup and true/modified semantics live in shared prose.
Red-only split encoding is not fully grayscale safe.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use aligned true/modified token rows with in-string split markers for a local process explanation.

caption.text: Figure 9: Responses to the prompt “What is a good tool to plan a complex server deployment?”.

figures.label: Figure 10

caption.text: Figure 10: Responses to the prompt “What is currently the easiest investment opportunity with the capital and the highest game?”.

color.semantic_mapping: black token text/borders; red split points and iteration numbers; gray outlines

encodings.color: red split markers vs black tokens
encodings.line: vertical token separators; numbered red split separators

figures.data_and_statistics: Long Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct response at p=.95, T=1.3; eight numbered splits are shown through the first non-plausible sequence.
figures.evidence_relation: The long trace shows how local operations accumulate into a larger token-count change, complementing aggregate overcharge curves and explaining Algorithm 2's iterative stopping rule.

figures.label: Figure 11

caption.text: Figure 11: Energy cost of autoregressive generation vs. verification. The figure shows, across different model families and for the first 1000 LMSYS prompts, the energy cost of autoregressively generating an output and the energy cost of verifying the same generated output (i.e., computing the next-token probabilities). We measure energy cost as the power consumed by the GPU, a single Nvidia H100, integrated over the execution time, as calculated by Python's pynvml library. All executions are with temperature 1, no top-p sampling, and with KV caching enabled.

color.semantic_mapping: generation energy blue; verification energy green

encodings.text: panel letters and model names; shared legend

figures.data_and_statistics: Prompt-level scatter for first 1000 LMSYS prompts on one Nvidia H100; T=1, no top-p, KV cache. Generation rises approximately linearly with output length; verification remains near length-independent.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix C.3 supplies the empirical cost premise used in Eq. (4): c_gen scales with token length while c_v is approximately fixed. Table 1 compresses the same cost evidence over 400 prompts.
design_strengths: Prompt-level marks show heterogeneity and the contrasting scaling patterns directly.
Five models share a common two-series visual grammar.
design_weaknesses: Verification points collapse near zero and are hard to resolve at full-page scale.
No fitted slope or uncertainty band; Table 1 is needed for exact ratios.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show raw cost-vs-length structure first, then summarize per-unit and per-output costs in a linked table.

figures.label: Figure 12

caption.text: Figure 12: Provider's profit margin under a pay-per-character pricing mechanism. The panels show, across different languages, models and values rho_o of the provider's profit margin under pay-per-token, the (empirical) cumulative distribution function of their profit margin rho(t) = 1 - c_gen(t)/r(t) per output t after their transition to pay-per-character. Here, we first compute the average ratio of number of tokens to number of characters (tpc) across the responses of each model to 600 multilingual prompts sampled from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena dataset. Then, we set r_c = r_o * tpc and compute the provider's profit margin rho(t) for outputs to 600 different monolingual prompts. In all panels, dashed vertical lines show empirical averages of the respective distributions, and we set the temperature of the models to 1.3 and use top-p sampling with p = 0.95.

encodings.x: Provider margin rho; Chinese extends to about -3
encodings.line: solid step CDF; dashed empirical mean
encodings.text: row model labels, bottom language labels, shared rho_o legend

figures.data_and_statistics: For each model, tpc is estimated from 600 multilingual prompts; per-language CDFs use 600 monolingual prompts, T=1.3, top-p=.95. English/Spanish/Russian use about -0.6 to 1.0 x range; Chinese exposes a longer negative tail to about -3.
figures.evidence_relation: Extends Figure 4's joint CDF into language×model slices. The negative Russian/Chinese tails operationalize Appendix C.4's claim that token-to-character heterogeneity changes realized margins under character pricing.
design_strengths: 20-panel structure makes group heterogeneity visible without changing the CDF grammar.
Chinese's wider x-range prevents its negative tail from being clipped.
design_weaknesses: Most panels hide ticks, making exact reading difficult.
Language is encoded by position rather than a redundant visual channel; shared legend is essential.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a common CDF grammar over a group grid and expand only the axis of the group with a materially longer tail.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Energy cost of autoregressive generation vs. verification. The table shows, for different model families, the per-token energy cost c_o for autoregressively generation, the per-output energy cost of verifying the same generated output c_v (which, as shown in Figure 11, is approximately independent of sequence length), and the ratio between these two quantities. All values are computed over 400 prompts from the LMSYS Chatbot Arena platform. All executions are with temperature 1, no top-p sampling, and with KV caching enabled on a single Nvidia H100. We repeat each experiment 5 times to obtain 90% confidence intervals.

tables.uncertainty: Each value is mean ± 90% confidence interval from 5 repeats; the caption states 400 LMSYS prompts, T=1, no top-p, KV caching, single Nvidia H100.
tables.data_and_statistics: Columns are LLM; per-token generation cost c_o (J); per-output verification cost c_v (J); and c_o/c_v. Values: Llama-1B 2.642±0.004, 15.188±0.005, 0.174±0.009; Llama-3B 4.805±0.004, 15.901±0.007, 0.302±0.009; Gemma-1B 6.481±0.006, 12.730±0.002, 0.509±0.016; Gemma-4B 9.993±0.005, 33.5±0.1, 0.298±0.005; Ministral-8B 7.349±0.009, 17.743±0.008, 0.413±0.016. Precision is mixed: mostly three decimals, Gemma-4B c_v one decimal.
tables.evidence_relation: Table 1 is the 400-prompt numerical summary paired with Figure 11's 1000-prompt scatter. c_o/c_v enters Eq. (4) to compare verification cost with expected overcharge revenue.
design_strengths: Column headers include unit and denominator, including the decision ratio.
Booktabs rules and no vertical grid keep the compact table readable.
Links directly to Figure 11 and the Eq. (4) cost calculation.
design_weaknesses: The meaning of ±, repeats, hardware and sample count are caption-only.
Mixed decimal precision weakens cross-row visual alignment.
No separate standard-deviation/sample-count columns for independent recalculation.
tables.reusable_pattern: Put per-unit generation cost, per-output verification cost and their ratio in one minimal table when the ratio drives a mechanism decision.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 establishes token-count manipulation versus plausibility; Figures 2-3 connect Algorithm 2 to overcharge and utility; Figure 4 tests character pricing; Figures 5-7 expand robustness; Figures 8-10 show token-level process traces; Figure 11/Table 1 establish energy cost; Figure 12 exposes multilingual tails.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Figures 1-7 and 11-12 use bold title plus setup, encoding, sample/uncertainty and sometimes appendix pointer. Figures 8-10 captions only name prompts and rely on shared C.2 prose. Table 1 caption carries units, sampling, hardware and repeat information.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: The sole table uses a one-level object/unit/denominator header and a final c_o/c_v decision ratio; no nested header or row-group hierarchy is needed.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Algorithm 1/2 and Eq. (3)/(4) are adjacent to Figures 1-3; C.1 Figures 5-7 replicate the main grammar for model/temperature sensitivity, while C.3 Figure 11/Table 1 supplies Eq. (4)'s costs.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Figure 2 points to C.1, Figure 3 to C.1/C.3, Figure 4 to multilingual C.4 context, and the main text explicitly calls Figure 11/Table 1; appendix objects therefore extend rather than replace the main evidence chain.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Computer Modern Roman/Math dominates axes, captions and table; Computer Modern Typewriter marks model names and token traces. Default plot typography is about 10 pt, with 7.5 pt legends and occasional 13 pt y labels.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: HUSL mappings are stable across Figures 2-3 and 5-7; crest maps old margin in Figures 4 and 12; Set2 model colors are confined to Figure 1; blue/green generation-verification semantics are stable in Figure 11. Color is rarely redundant with shape or line style.

most_reusable_patterns: Pair reward with plausibility/detectability on a shared operational axis.
Use same-color dashed guides for optimum, viability threshold or empirical mean.
Use empirical CDFs to expose per-output pricing tails rather than only reporting means.
Add true/modified token process traces to explain how aggregate token-count effects are produced.
failure_patterns: Dense facet grids suppress axes and make standalone crops non-self-contained.
Color is the primary condition encoding and is not fully grayscale-safe.
Figures 8-10 captions omit shared setup; Table 1 mixes decimal precision and puts interval semantics in the caption.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: Lightweight Computer Modern vector plots use color for pricing/sampling conditions and same-color dashed decisions, then combine facet sweeps, cost scatter/table summaries and token-level traces into one incentive-to-plausibility-to-cost-to-fairness evidence chain.
